live_cases.name: University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC

case.why_ai_cites_it: The controlling answer to AI-invented subject matter: whatever a system devises, the application must name a human inventor. Companies cite it when structuring filings around human contributors; challengers cite it to attack patents where the human contribution looks nominal.

reading.body:
Thaler v. Vidal settled that an AI system cannot be named as an inventor, but left open how much AI assistance a human inventor may use.

The Federal Circuit decided the case on the statutory word "individual," holding that an inventor under the Patent Act must be a natural person. It did not reach whether the system in question conceived anything, so the ruling is about who can be named, not about what a machine can do. The court expressly reserved the question of how much AI assistance a human inventor may receive.

That reservation is where the practical risk sits. A patent application must name a human inventor, and the doctrine is cited both by companies structuring filings around human contributors and by challengers attacking patents where the human contribution looks nominal. The dispute has moved from machine inventorship, which is closed, to inventorship quality, which is not.

The data covers one appellate holding, one citation, and one live case citing it, University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC. It does not establish a threshold for sufficient human contribution, and no such threshold appears in the record here. Nothing in this data ties the question to compute, buildings, or power.

The holding turns on a word, not on a machine. Because the court read "individual" to mean a natural person, it never had to decide whether the system conceived anything, which means the opinion supplies no test for conception at all. Every downstream dispute therefore inherits a gap: the statute names who may be an inventor, and nothing in this record says how much a named human must actually have done.

That gap is asymmetric in practice. A company drafting a filing can point to a human contributor and satisfy the naming requirement on its face, while a challenger must argue that the named contribution was nominal. The data records both postures as live uses of the same precedent, which is why the case reads as settled and contested at once. The closed question is who can be named. The open question is whether the naming is honest.

The single live case in the data, University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC, is the only signal here about where the quality question is being litigated. One case is not a trend, and the data does not say what contribution is alleged in it. What the data does establish is that the reserved question has already been carried into a proceeding, which is the step that turns a reservation in an opinion into a fact pattern a court must eventually address.

What did Thaler v. Vidal actually decide?
The Federal Circuit held that an inventor under the Patent Act must be a natural person, so an application naming an AI system as the sole inventor is properly refused. It did not decide whether the system conceived anything.

Can an AI system be named as an inventor on a patent?
No. The court read the statutory word "individual" to require a natural person, which closes machine inventorship.

How much AI assistance can a human inventor use?
The data does not hold a threshold. The court expressly left the question open, and no answer appears in this record.

What is the difference between machine inventorship and inventorship quality?
Machine inventorship asks whether a system can be named, and that is closed. Inventorship quality asks whether the named human's contribution is sufficient, and that remains unsettled.

Which live case cites this holding?
University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC, the only live case in this data, with a total of one.

Does this data connect the inventorship question to compute, buildings, or power?
No. Nothing in this record ties the holding or the reserved question to compute, buildings, or power.
